fig2_curves_reach: Sand: its retention curve drops almost to zero within a few tens of centimetres of suction, because its pores are nearly all the same size (large n = 2.68).
Silty clay loam: the curve falls slowly over five decades of suction, because its pores span many sizes (small n = 1.23).
The dashed line is the constant kappa = 3.47e-10: the relative conductivity at which a crop can no longer dry the soil at the sensor.
The reach of sand (199 cm) is where its conductivity curve crosses kappa; the steep curve crosses early.
The reach of silty clay loam (128 260 cm): its gentle curve crosses kappa only far in the dry range.
Each point is the reach of one soil from Eq. (4); the reach falls as n grows. The three lines are Eq. (4) for three values of alpha: a smaller alpha gives a longer reach.
Grey band: the range of triggers tested in the simulations (50 to 10 000 cm). Soils whose reach lies inside the band have a trigger beyond which irrigation stops.
fig3_trigger_reach: Sand: irrigation falls to zero at 100 to 150 cm. Every drier trigger, including the common 300 cm, is never reached.
Silty clay loam still irrigates at 10 000 cm, because its conductivity fades slowly and the crop can keep drying the soil.
The dashed line is the reach (trigger / reach = 1). On this scaled axis every soil stops irrigating between 0.5 and 1.
Sand: the bar is the observed interval (100 to 150 cm) and the dot its lower end; the prediction of Eq. (4) (199 cm) lies within a factor of two.
An arrow means that even the driest trigger tested (10 000 cm) still fired, so only a lower bound of the reach is known.
Grey band: within a factor of two of the 1:1 line (black). Points in the band are predicted well.
Sand beyond its reach: the yield stays at the rainfed value (1.13 Mg/ha) because the field is never irrigated.
fig4_marginal_fate: Sandy loam transpires the largest share of each irrigation millimetre (0.64): it holds the water near the roots and loses little to the surface.
Coarse sand: drainage below 1 m is the largest single loss (0.32), because the soil passes extra water on before the crop can use it.
Overhead irrigation: the transpired share is negative (-0.08). Water intercepted by the canopy evaporates with the energy that would have driven transpiration.
Most of the overhead water (0.79) leaves as other evaporation: canopy interception, ponds and litter.
Subsurface application transpires most (0.51) but also drains most (0.23), because it wets the profile from within.
fig5_dose: Plateau of coarse sand (0.45): the share of a large dose that drains. It is set by the soil, which passes water on fast.
Doses of 1 to 2 mm hardly drain (0.01 to 0.09): they are used near the surface on the day they are applied.
The dose scale d_D (about 4 mm in every soil): at d = d_D the drained share reaches 63 % of its plateau. It is about one day of crop water use.
The transpired share rises with the dose and peaks at 15 to 20 mm, because less of a larger dose is lost from the wet surface.
At 1 mm, 60 to 72 % of the dose evaporates: small doses trade drainage for evaporation.
fig1_concept: One millimetre of irrigation applied to the surface; the arrows that leave the column are its fates, with widths in proportion to their shares.
Transpiration (0.38 of each millimetre): the only fate that makes yield.
Soil evaporation (0.25): water evaporated from the wetted surface with the energy also available to the crop.
Other evaporation (0.19): intercepted water, ponds and litter.
Drainage below 1 m (0.16): water lost to the crop that also carries nitrate.
The sensor at 20 cm: irrigation starts when the suction it reads exceeds the trigger.
The reach of sand (199 cm), where its conductivity has collapsed; the usual triggers lie beyond it.
Grey band: the triggers usually tabulated (300 to 600 cm).
